content: Snakebite envenoming is a neglected tropical disease (NTD) that causes significant suffering, disability, and premature death across all continents. Each year, there are approximately 7 million cases of envenoming, resulting in 81,000 to 138,000 deaths. The economic burden of snakebite envenoming is immense, particularly in lowand middle-income countries where social security systems are often lacking. This burden extends beyond the victims to their families, especially in impoverished communities. As part of the global effort to achieve Universal Health Coverage (UHC) by 2030, immediate action is required to alleviate the suffering caused by snakebite envenoming. Many countries have called for a coordinated response to address this issue. Following recommendations from the World Health Organization’s (WHO) Strategic and Technical Advisory Group for Neglected Tropical Diseases and a resolution adopted by the 71st World Health Assembly in 2018, snakebite envenoming has been added to WHO’s list of Category A NTDs. WHO has since developed a comprehensive strategy to reduce mortality and disability from snakebite envenoming by 50% by 2030. This strategy outlines actions to be taken at the national level, supported by regional collaboration, to save lives and prevent unnecessary suffering. For millions of people worldwide, the risk of snakebite is a daily concern during routine activities such as walking to school, tending gardens, herding livestock, fetching water, or even using the toilet. A single misstep or moment of inattention can result in a potentially fatal encounter. Addressing this problem begins with improving community education about snakebite risks, encouraging individuals to seek healthcare, and ensuring effective case management for all patients. The strategy emphasizes the importance of first aid, affordable and effective treatment provided by well-trained medical staff, and rehabilitation to help victims recover and return to productive lives. The ultimate goal is to improve care for all patients, thereby reducing deaths and disabilities by 50% before 2030. To achieve this, four strategic aims have been identified: 1. Empowering and Engaging Communities: Efforts will focus on preventing snakebite envenoming and increasing the use of treatment through education, training, and facilitation. Research will explore sociocultural, economic, political, and geographical factors influencing perceptions of snakebite and treatment-seeking behavior. These findings will inform changes in behavior, policy, and practice. 2. Ensuring Safe and Effective Treatment: A stable and sustainable market for safe, effective, and affordable antivenoms will be developed. Antivenom production and quality must meet internationally accepted standards through collaboration among academia, industry, and public and private institutions. 3. Strengthening Health Systems: Using the principles of the WHO Health Systems Framework, snakebite prevention, treatment, and management will be integrated into national health systems, plans, and policy frameworks. 4. Increasing Partnerships, Coordination, and Resources: Strong collaboration will be essential for implementing this comprehensive plan. Advocacy will be necessary to build a global coalition to drive change, generate investment, implement projects, and accelerate research into new therapies, diagnostics, and medical interventions. Emphasis will be placed on building country capacity and facilitating knowledge exchange. The strategy will be implemented incrementally, starting with pilot testing in 10–12 high-burden countries during 2019–2020. These countries will receive support to design and implement locally relevant plans and participate in regional initiatives. During the scaling-up phase (2021–2024), an additional 35–40 countries will be involved as resources increase and the strategy’s effectiveness is demonstrated. By the full roll-out phase (2025–2030), all countries will be able to integrate the strategy into their public health agendas. Through advocacy, WHO aims to build a sustainable global coalition committed to achieving the targets and milestones necessary to halve the number of snakebite deaths and disabilities by 2030. This strategy represents a critical step toward addressing the global burden of snakebite envenoming and improving the lives of affected individuals and communities.
